title: Container and Kubernetes security
summary: How containers and clusters get breached and defended: image and build hygiene, pod hardening, the API request path, RBAC, admission, network policy, Secrets, exposed APIs, runc escapes and detection.
outcomes: Explain why containers share one kernel and list the paths from a compromised pod to the node, the cluster and the cloud
Fix a Dockerfile and a pod spec: non-root, no secrets in layers, digest pinning, drop ALL, seccomp, read-only root
Trace an API request through authentication, authorization and admission, and write least-privilege RBAC
Write default-deny NetworkPolicies and enforce Pod Security Standards with namespace labels
Explain why base64 Secrets are not encrypted and configure encryption at rest with KMS
Describe the Tesla, Hildegard, IngressNightmare, runc and Leaky Vessels cases and the control that breaks each
Combine Kubernetes audit logs and Falco rules to detect what each alone would miss

lessons.title: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model

blocks.md:
Start with a plain picture. A company runs a web shop, a payment service and a log collector as three containers on one machine. An attacker finds a bug in the web shop and can now run commands inside its container. The question this whole course answers is: **what else can they reach from there, and what stops them?**

A **threat model** is the written answer to "who might attack, what do they want, and which paths could they take". For containers the answer starts from one fact: every container on a machine is an ordinary Linux process running on the **same kernel**.

Recall from the prerequisite courses: a container is a process with **namespaces** (its own view of process IDs, mounts, network and users), **cgroups** (limits on CPU and memory), a reduced set of **capabilities** (root's powers split into pieces), a **seccomp** filter (a list of allowed system calls) and an **LSM** profile (Linux Security Module, such as AppArmor or SELinux, which adds mandatory access rules). Each is a fence drawn by the kernel. None of them is a second kernel.

That is the difference from a virtual machine (VM), which runs its own guest kernel on virtual hardware. A VM escape needs a bug in the hypervisor, a small target. A container escape needs a bug in the shared kernel, the container runtime, or a fence someone forgot to put up. The kernel's system call interface is huge by comparison.

blocks.title: What a compromised container can try to reach

scenes.caption: Normal state. Three containers on one node share one kernel. The node also holds the kubelet's credentials and can reach the cloud metadata service and the cluster's API server.
The attacker gets code execution inside the web container through an application bug. So far they hold only what that process holds: its files, its network view, its token if one was mounted.
Path 1, the network: by default every pod can connect to every other pod, so the payment service and the API server are one connection away.
Path 2, credentials: a mounted service account token or a reachable metadata service turns a code bug into API or cloud access. No escape needed.

Path 3, the escape: a kernel or runtime bug, or a risky setting such as a privileged container, lets the process act on the host itself. Now every container, the host files and the kubelet's credentials are in reach.
The defender's job is to make each path long: segment the network, mount no credentials that are not needed, and keep the fences on so an escape needs a fresh, unpatched bug.

blocks.md:
An **escape** (also called a breakout) means a process that should be confined to its container gains the ability to act on the host: read or write host files, run processes outside its namespaces, or control other containers. It does not have to be dramatic. Mounting the host's root directory into a container is an escape by configuration; nobody exploited anything.

It helps to sort container risks by **where they enter**:

1. **Image**: vulnerable or malicious software baked in before the container ever runs.
2. **Build**: secrets and untrusted downloads that end up in layers.
3. **Runtime settings**: privileged mode, host mounts, host namespaces, extra capabilities.
4. **Orchestrator**: who may talk to the Kubernetes API, the kubelet and etcd (the cluster database), and with what rights.
5. **Network**: which pods can reach which.
6. **Host and runtime bugs**: kernel, runc, and containerd or CRI-O (the daemons that pull images and run containers on nodes).

The lessons follow that order, then add detection and real escape cases.

blocks.code:
# On the host
uname -r
6.8.0-45-generic

# Inside any container on that host
docker run --rm alpine uname -r
6.8.0-45-generic
blocks.caption: Each command is followed by its output. The kernel version is the same inside and outside, because there is only one kernel. The version string here is an example; yours will differ, but it will always match between host and container. (A VM would report its own guest kernel.)

blocks.md: Misconception: "root in a container is harmless because it is only container root". Without user namespaces, UID 0 inside the container is UID 0 on the host, held back only by dropped capabilities, seccomp and the LSM. Remove those fences, or find a bug in them, and it is real root.
A container is a fenced process on a shared kernel. Threat-model it as "attacker has a shell in this process" and ask which credentials, network paths and kernel interfaces that shell can touch.

blocks.question: An attacker has code execution in a pod that runs as non-root, has no extra capabilities and no host mounts, but has the default service account token mounted and network access to the API server. What is the most realistic next step?
options: Use the mounted token to call the Kubernetes API with whatever rights that service account has
Escape to the host through the shared kernel immediately
Read other containers' memory through the cgroup
Nothing; non-root containers are fully isolated
blocks.explain: No fence was removed, so an escape needs a fresh kernel or runtime bug. The token is free: it is a credential sitting in the filesystem, and the API server is reachable. Its rights decide the blast radius, which is why RBAC and automount settings matter (lessons 8 and 9).

blocks.question: Why is a container escape usually considered easier to find than a VM escape?
options: Containers share the host kernel, whose large system call interface is directly reachable, while a VM's guest talks to a much smaller hypervisor interface
blocks.explain: A container's processes make system calls straight into the host kernel, so any kernel bug reachable through those calls is a candidate. A VM's kernel is separate; escaping needs a bug in the hypervisor's narrower interface.

lessons.title: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning

blocks.md:
Every image starts with a `FROM` line naming a **base image**: the operating system files your application sits on. A typical `debian` or `ubuntu` base brings a shell, a package manager, core utilities and hundreds of libraries. Your web app may use five of them. The rest are still there at runtime.

That matters twice. First, every extra program is a tool an attacker can use after a foothold: a shell to run commands, `curl` to download more tools, a package manager to install them. Second, every extra package carries its own security advisories, so the list of known vulnerabilities in your image grows with code you never call.

A **minimal image** keeps only what the application needs. Google's [distroless](https://github.com/GoogleContainerTools/distroless) images go furthest. The name means "without the distribution": the README describes them as containing only the application and its runtime dependencies, and states that they "do not contain package managers, shells or any other programs you would expect to find in a standard Linux distribution".

The README gives sizes: the smallest, `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian13`, is around 2 MiB, about half the size of Alpine (around 5 MiB) and less than 2% of Debian (124 MiB). Alpine Linux is a small distribution built on the musl C library and BusyBox, a single binary that provides many small Unix tools. Each distroless image also has a `nonroot` tag that runs as an unprivileged user, and a `debug` tag that adds a BusyBox shell for troubleshooting only.

blocks.title: Base image size (MiB), from the distroless README

scenes.caption: Sizes as the distroless README states them. Size is a proxy for how much software, and how many potential CVEs and attacker tools, ship with your app.
The point is not disk space. A 2 MiB static image has no shell for an attacker to use after exploiting your app, and almost no packages for a scanner to flag.

blocks.md: The standard pattern to get there is a **multi-stage build**: one stage has the compiler and build tools, a final stage copies only the built program into a minimal base. Nothing from the build stage reaches the final image unless you copy it.

blocks.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.27 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/app .

# Final stage: no shell, no package manager, runs as an unprivileged user
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian13:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
blocks.caption: A Go service built in a full image and shipped in distroless. CGO_ENABLED=0 makes a static binary that needs no C library. ENTRYPOINT uses the list form because, as the distroless README notes, there is no shell to interpret a plain string.

blocks.md:
Next, **scanning**. An image scanner reads the list of packages in each layer (from the package manager's database and from language lock files), then matches name and version against vulnerability databases of **CVEs** (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, the public catalogue that gives each known flaw an ID such as CVE-2024-21626). [Trivy](https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy), an open source scanner from Aqua Security, is a common choice; it also finds embedded secrets and misconfigurations, and can emit an **SBOM** (software bill of materials: a machine-readable list of every component in the image).

Scanners have known limits. They see packages, not behaviour: a statically linked binary copied in without metadata may be invisible. A finding means "this version is listed as affected", not "this is exploitable here". And an image clean today gains CVEs tomorrow as new advisories are published, so scan in CI (continuous integration: the automated pipeline that builds and tests every change) and keep rescanning what is running.

blocks.prompt: A team switches from `debian` to distroless and the scanner's finding count drops from 140 to 3. Does that mean the application is 47 times more secure?
blocks.reveal: No. Most of the 140 findings were in packages the application never called, so the real risk reduction is smaller than the number suggests. What did change is real, though: the noise drop lets people act on the 3 that matter, and an attacker who exploits the app finds no shell, no `curl` and no package manager to continue with. The application's own bugs are untouched by the base image.

blocks.md: Misconception: "we scan, so our images are safe". A scanner only knows published vulnerabilities in recognised packages. It does not find your own code's bugs, a backdoored but unlisted dependency, or a secret left in a layer unless a secret scanner runs too.
Ship the least software that runs your app: multi-stage builds into a minimal or distroless base, scanned in CI and rescanned while running.

blocks.question: A distroless image has no shell. What is the most important security effect of that?
options: It prevents the kernel from running system calls
It makes the image impossible to exploit
After exploiting the app, an attacker has no ready interpreter or tools inside the container to continue with
blocks.explain: The app can still have bugs, but the classic next step (open a shell, download tools) has nothing to work with. It raises the attacker's cost; it does not remove the need to patch the app.

blocks.question: Your scanner reports no vulnerabilities for an image built last month. What should you conclude?
options: No currently published advisory matches a package the scanner recognised; rescan regularly because new CVEs are published every day
Scanning is unnecessary for this image
blocks.explain: A scan is a snapshot against today's databases and only covers packages it can identify. New advisories appear constantly, so running images need continuous rescanning.

lessons.title: Dockerfile mistakes: root, secrets in layers, unverified downloads

blocks.md:
A **Dockerfile** is the recipe that builds an image, one instruction per line. Three mistakes in it show up again and again in incident reports, and each has a simple fix.

1. **Running as root.** If no `USER` instruction appears, the container's process runs as UID 0.
2. **Secrets in layers.** A credential copied in or passed as a build argument stays in the image, even if a later line deletes it.
3. **Unverified downloads.** Fetching code from a URL at build time trusts whatever that server returns that day.

blocks.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.12
# mistake 2: build args persist in the image
ARG PYPI_TOKEN
# copies everything in the folder, including .env
COPY . /app
RUN pip install --index-url https://user:${PYPI_TOKEN}@pypi.example.com/simple -r /app/requirements.txt
# mistake 2: the file is still in the COPY layer
RUN rm /app/.env
# mistake 3: remote download with no checksum
ADD https://example.com/tool.tar.gz /opt/
# mistake 1: no USER instruction, so this runs as root
CMD python /app/main.py
blocks.caption: The vulnerable version. Each comment marks a mistake explained below. (Dockerfile comments must sit on their own lines.)

blocks.md:
Why does `rm` not remove the secret? Recall from the containers course: each instruction produces a **layer**, a tar archive of the changes it made, and layers are stacked. Deleting a file in a later layer adds a **whiteout** marker that hides it in the merged view. The earlier layer's tar, which contains the file in full, is still part of the image and is downloaded by anyone who can pull it.

Docker's [build secrets guide](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/secrets/) is explicit about the other half: "Build arguments and environment variables are inappropriate for passing secrets to your build, because they persist in the final image." Anyone with the image can read them from its history or config.

blocks.title: A deleted file still ships in the lower layer

scenes.caption: Layer 1 (COPY) adds the app, its requirements and a .env file holding a cloud key. Each layer is stored as its own tar blob.
Layer 2 (RUN rm) cannot edit layer 1. It records a whiteout for .env, a marker that hides the name in the stacked view.
The merged view a running container sees has no .env. This is what fools people into thinking it is gone.
But the image still contains layer 1's tar. Anyone who pulls the image can extract that blob and read the key. Exactly this happened to Codecov in 2021.

blocks.md:
**Real case: Codecov, 2021.** Codecov is a service that measures test coverage; customers ran its Bash Uploader script in their CI (continuous integration) pipelines. In its [post-mortem](https://about.codecov.io/apr-2021-post-mortem/) the company wrote that the attacker "was able to extract an HMAC key for a Google Cloud Storage service account from an intermediate layer" of its public self-hosted Docker image. (HMAC, hash-based message authentication code, keys here act as storage credentials.) With it the attacker altered the hosted uploader script so that it sent CI environment variables, often full of secrets, to the attacker.

A customer caught it on April 1, 2021 by comparing the script's SHA-256 checksum against the one published on GitHub. Codecov's fixes: revoke and rotate keys, rebuild every public image as squashed or multi-stage so intermediate layers never ship, and publish a signed, checksum-verifiable uploader.

blocks.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
# fix 2: the token is mounted only for this RUN and never written to a layer
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pypi_token \
    pip install --target /deps \
      --index-url "https://user:$(cat /run/secrets/pypi_token)@pypi.example.com/simple" \
      -r requirements.txt
# fix 3: pin the download to a known checksum, unpack it in the build stage
ADD --checksum=sha256:<expected-sha256> https://example.com/tool.tar.gz /tmp/tool.tar.gz
RUN mkdir -p /opt/tool && tar -xzf /tmp/tool.tar.gz -C /opt/tool

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /deps /deps
COPY --from=build /opt/tool /opt/tool
COPY main.py .
ENV PYTHONPATH=/deps
# fix 1: run as an unprivileged, explicit UID
USER 10001:10001
CMD ["python", "/app/main.py"]
blocks.caption: Fixed. Build with: docker build --secret id=pypi_token,env=PYPI_TOKEN . The secret mount follows Docker's build secrets guide; ADD --checksum is the verification Docker's best-practices page recommends for remote files; a .dockerignore listing .env keeps it out of COPY entirely.

blocks.md:
Why each fix works:

- **Secret mounts** (`RUN --mount=type=secret`) expose the secret as a file under `/run/secrets/` only while that one `RUN` executes. It is never part of a layer, the image config or the build history.
- **Multi-stage** means only what you `COPY --from` reaches the final image, so even a mistake in the build stage stays out of what you ship.
- **`ADD --checksum`** makes the build fail if the downloaded bytes do not hash to the value you pinned. Docker's [best practices](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/best-practices/) page says ADD has built-in checksum validation for remote resources. Without it, whoever controls that URL controls part of your image. For local files, prefer `COPY`, which does nothing clever.
- **`USER 10001`** sets a non-root UID. The same page recommends `USER` whenever a service can run without privileges, and an explicit UID because otherwise the number assigned can change between rebuilds.

Defender view. Prevent: secret mounts, multi-stage builds, `.dockerignore`, a CI check that fails on `USER` missing or `ADD` without `--checksum`. Detect: run a secret scanner over every layer of every pushed image, not just the final filesystem. Respond: a secret that ever reached a pushed layer is compromised. Rotate it; deleting the image does not un-publish copies already pulled.

blocks.question: A Dockerfile has `COPY id_rsa /root/.ssh/` on line 4 and `RUN rm /root/.ssh/id_rsa` on line 9. The final container has no key file. Is the key exposed?
options: Yes: the layer from line 4 still contains the file, and anyone who can pull the image can extract that layer
Only if the image is pushed to Docker Hub with the latest tag
Only if the container runs as root
blocks.explain: Line 9's layer only adds a whiteout. The earlier layer is immutable and ships with the image. Use a secret or SSH mount instead, and rotate the key now.

blocks.question: Why is `ARG API_KEY` followed by `RUN curl -H "key: $API_KEY" ...` a leak even though no file is written?
options: Build arguments are recorded in the image's metadata and history, so the value persists in the final image
It is not a leak if the build runs in CI
blocks.explain: Docker's guide says build arguments and environment variables persist in the final image. Use `--mount=type=secret` so the value is available only during that RUN.

lessons.title: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission

blocks.md:
When a pod spec says `image: shop/web:1.4`, which bytes run? The answer depends on the registry at the moment of pulling. A **tag** such as `1.4` or `latest` is a movable name. Docker's [best practices](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/best-practices/) page says it directly: "Image tags are mutable, meaning a publisher can update a tag to point to a new image."

A **digest** is different. Recall from the containers course that it is the SHA-256 hash of the image manifest, written like `sha256:a8560b...`. Change one byte and the digest changes. Referring to an image by digest therefore pins exact content.

blocks.code:
# Tag only: rebuilds may get different bytes
FROM alpine:3.21

# Tag plus digest: always the same image, and the tag stays readable
FROM alpine:3.21@sha256:a8560b36e8b8210634f77d9f7f9efd7ffa463e380b75e2e74aff4511df3ef88c
blocks.caption: The example Docker's best-practices page uses. When both are present, the digest wins; the tag is just a label for humans.

blocks.md:
Pinning answers "is this the same image as before?" It does not answer "did my build system produce it?". For that you **sign** images. **Sigstore** is an open source project, now under the OpenSSF (Open Source Security Foundation), that makes signing cheap; **Cosign** is its tool for container images.

Sigstore's [overview](https://docs.sigstore.dev/about/overview/) describes "keyless" signing: Cosign makes a fresh key pair, proves who is signing with an **OIDC** (OpenID Connect, a standard way to say "this identity token was issued by that provider") token from, for example, a CI system, and gets a short-lived certificate from Sigstore's certificate authority, **Fulcio**. The signature is recorded in **Rekor**, a public append-only transparency log. A verifier checks the signature, that the certificate names the expected identity, and that the entry is in the log. No long-lived private key exists to steal.

blocks.code:
# In CI, after pushing: sign the exact digest (keyless, using the CI's OIDC identity)
cosign sign registry.example.com/shop/web@sha256:<digest>

# Anyone can verify, stating which identity must have signed
cosign verify gcr.io/distroless/static-debian13 \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://accounts.google.com \
  --certificate-identity keyless@distroless.iam.gserviceaccount.com
blocks.caption: The verify line is the command the distroless README gives for checking its own images. Verifying without stating the expected identity proves only that someone signed, not that the right party did.

blocks.md:
Signing helps only if something **refuses unsigned images**. In Kubernetes that is an **admission controller** (lesson 7 explains admission in full): code in the API server's request path that can reject an object before it is stored. Policy engines such as Kyverno (a Kubernetes policy engine, lesson 10) provide image verification: its [ImageValidatingPolicy](https://kyverno.io/docs/policy-types/image-validating-policy/) checks each pod's images against required signatures or attestations, and with `mutateDigest: true` rewrites tags to digests so the image verified is the image that runs.

An **attestation** is signed metadata about an artifact, for example "this image was built by this pipeline from this commit" or "this SBOM describes it". **SLSA** (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts, pronounced "salsa") is a framework of such provenance requirements; it is useful to know the name.

blocks.title: From commit to running pod: where each control sits

scenes.caption: The path an image takes. Every hop is a place an attacker could swap content: the build machine, the registry, or the tag itself.
An attacker with registry write access pushes a malicious image and moves the tag 1.4 to it. A pod spec that names only the tag will pull the new bytes.
Pinning the digest in the pod spec means the node asks for exact content. The moved tag is ignored, and a byte-level change cannot match the hash.

CI signs the digest with its OIDC identity and the signature is logged in Rekor. The admission policy refuses any image not signed by that CI identity, so even a new, correctly hashed malicious image is rejected.
What remains: a compromised CI pipeline signs malicious images with a valid identity. Signing moves trust to the build system, so the build system must be protected like production.

blocks.md: Misconception: "a signature means the image is safe". A signature proves who produced it and that it was not changed since. A signed image can still contain vulnerable packages or a backdoor that entered upstream, as in the xz-utils case from the Linux course. Combine signing with scanning and provenance.
Pin by digest so you always run the same bytes; sign in CI and verify at admission so you only run bytes your pipeline produced.

blocks.question: A pod spec uses `image: shop/web:1.4`. The image was signed and scanned when 1.4 was first pushed. What risk remains?
options: The tag can later be pointed at different bytes, which were never scanned, and no signature check runs unless admission enforces it
The kubelet re-verifies signatures on every pull by default
blocks.explain: Signing at push time does nothing unless something verifies at deploy time, and a tag can be moved. Pin the digest and enforce signature verification in admission.

blocks.question: Why does keyless signing reduce one big risk of classic signing?
options: There is no long-lived private key to steal; each signature uses a short-lived certificate tied to an OIDC identity and recorded in a public log
It does not need a network
blocks.explain: Classic signing depends on guarding one private key for years. Keyless signing ties each signature to an identity at that moment, and the transparency log lets identity owners spot misuse.

lessons.title: Runtime settings that switch the fences off

blocks.md:
The fences from lesson 1 are on by default. A handful of settings in a pod spec, or flags to `docker run`, switch them off again, usually because some tool "needed it to work". Each one turns an application bug into host access without any exploit at all.

Here is a pod spec that a monitoring or debugging tool might ship with. Read it as an attacker would: what does a shell in this container get?

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: node-debug
spec:
  hostPID: true
  hostNetwork: true
  containers:
  - name: tools
    image: registry.example.com/tools:1.0
    securityContext:
      privileged: true
      capabilities:
        add: ["SYS_ADMIN"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: host-root
      mountPath: /host
    - name: docker-sock
      mountPath: /var/run/docker.sock
  volumes:
  - name: host-root
    hostPath:
      path: /
  - name: docker-sock
    hostPath:
      path: /var/run/docker.sock
blocks.caption: Every risky setting at once. privileged, the hostPath of / or the Docker socket alone is enough to take over the node; the others each open part of it. All of them are rejected by the Baseline Pod Security Standard (lesson 10).

blocks.md:
Setting by setting, using the Kubernetes documentation's own wording where it exists:

- **`privileged: true`**. The [Linux kernel security constraints](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/linux-kernel-security-constraints/) page says privileged containers "are given all Linux capabilities", run with the Unconfined seccomp profile overriding any you set, ignore AppArmor profiles, and run as SELinux's `unconfined_t` domain. All four fences at once.
- **`capabilities.add: ["SYS_ADMIN"]`**. `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` is the broad capability behind mounting filesystems and many other administrative operations; adding it hands back much of what dropping root's powers took away.
- **`hostPath` of `/`**. The host's root filesystem appears at `/host`. The RBAC good-practices page warns that unrestricted host filesystem access allows "reading data from other containers, and abusing the credentials of system services, such as Kubelet."

- **The Docker socket**. `/var/run/docker.sock` is the Unix socket the Docker daemon listens on, and the daemon runs as root. Docker's [post-install guide](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/linux-postinstall/) warns that even membership of the `docker` group "grants root-level privileges", and its security page explains why: whoever controls the daemon can start a new container with the host's `/` mounted inside. A mounted runtime socket is root on the node by another name. The same holds for any container runtime's control socket.
- **`hostPID: true`**. The container joins the node's PID namespace, so it sees every process on the node, including their command lines, which often carry secrets.
- **`hostNetwork: true`**. The pod uses the node's network stack: it can bind node ports and reach services listening only on the node. The Network Policies page says policy behaviour for hostNetwork pods is undefined, and AWS's EKS documentation notes such pods always have access to the instance metadata service.

blocks.title: Each setting opens a different door to the node

scenes.caption: A normal container: it talks to the kernel through its fences and sees only its own filesystem, processes and network namespace.
privileged: true. All capabilities, seccomp and LSM profiles off. The kernel interface is wide open; device access and mounts become possible.
hostPath /. No kernel trick needed: the host's files, including other pods' data and the kubelet's credentials, are just a directory away.
Runtime socket mounted. The container asks the root daemon to start a new, fully privileged container with the host filesystem attached. The daemon does what it is told.
hostPID and hostNetwork. The container shares the node's process list and network stack: it can read other processes' command lines and reach node-local services and the metadata endpoint.

Defender view: Baseline Pod Security forbids every one of these; Falco ships rules that flag privileged containers and sensitive mounts at runtime; a node-level agent that truly needs them runs in its own locked-down namespace.

blocks.prompt: A CI system runs builds inside a pod and mounts the node's Docker socket so builds can run `docker build`. Every developer can push a branch that runs in CI. Who effectively has root on that node?
blocks.reveal: Every developer who can push a branch. A build step can talk to the mounted socket and ask the root daemon to start any container, including one with the host's `/` mounted. The usual fixes are rootless or daemonless builders (tools such as Buildah that build images without a root-owned daemon), separate throwaway build nodes or VMs, and never mixing these pods with production workloads on the same node.

blocks.md: Defender view. Prevent: enforce the Baseline (better, Restricted) Pod Security Standard everywhere, and give genuine node agents their own namespace with a reviewed exemption. Detect: alert on pods created with privileged, hostPID, hostNetwork or hostPath in the API audit log, and on runtime-socket access with Falco. Respond: treat the node as compromised if such a pod ran untrusted code; rotate the kubelet's and node's credentials.

privileged, extra capabilities, hostPath, runtime sockets, hostPID and hostNetwork each turn a container back into a process on the host. If a workload asks for one, ask why, and isolate it if the answer is real.

blocks.question: Which single setting gives a container control equivalent to root on the node without any kernel or runtime bug?
options: Mounting the container runtime's socket, such as /var/run/docker.sock
blocks.explain: The runtime daemon runs as root and will start whatever container it is asked to, including one with the host filesystem mounted. Docker documents that even docker group membership is root-level access.

blocks.question: A team says their pod needs `privileged: true` only to change one network setting. What is the better request?
options: Disable seccomp but keep capabilities default
Keep privileged; it is the same thing
Add only the specific capability needed (for example NET_ADMIN) and keep seccomp, AppArmor or SELinux on
blocks.explain: The Kubernetes docs advise granting specific capabilities rather than privileged mode, because privileged also removes seccomp and LSM confinement and grants every capability.

lessons.title: A hardened pod spec, line by line

blocks.md: Now the opposite direction. Start with the shortest pod spec that works, and look at what it silently allows. Then add the settings that put each fence back, and see why each one matters.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: registry.example.com/shop/web:1.4
blocks.caption: Before: valid, common, and permissive by default.

blocks.md:
What that minimal spec gets, according to the Kubernetes documentation:

- It runs as whatever user the image declares, which is **root** if the Dockerfile had no `USER`.
- `allowPrivilegeEscalation` **defaults to true**. The [security context](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/security-context/) page explains that this field controls the kernel's `no_new_privs` flag, inverted: when it is true, a process can gain privileges by running a setuid program (recall setuid from the Linux course).
- **seccomp is Unconfined** unless the kubelet runs with the `seccompDefault` option; the [seccomp tutorial](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/security/seccomp/) says "Otherwise, the default is Unconfined." This surprises people, because plain Docker applies its default profile, which its docs say disables around 44 system calls out of 300+.
- The service account **token is mounted** automatically (lesson 9).
- The root filesystem is **writable**, so an attacker can drop tools anywhere.

blocks.title: Each line of a hardened spec and the fence it restores
blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  hostUsers: false
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    runAsGroup: 10001
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: registry.example.com/shop/web@sha256:<digest>
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
    resources:
      limits:
        memory: "256Mi"
      requests:
        cpu: "250m"
        memory: "256Mi"
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}

scenes.caption: Do not mount an API token unless the app calls the Kubernetes API. Most web apps never do.
Run in a user namespace: UID 0 inside maps to an unprivileged UID on the host. Needs node support (Linux 6.3 or later with idmap mounts, per the docs).
Refuse to start if the image would run as root, and run as a fixed non-root UID and GID.
Apply the container runtime's default seccomp profile instead of Unconfined. Dangerous, rarely needed system calls now fail.
Set no_new_privs: setuid binaries can no longer raise privileges.
Root filesystem read-only: an attacker cannot drop tools or modify the app's files.
Drop every capability. A web server on a port above 1024 needs none.
Memory limit and requests: a compromised or buggy pod cannot starve the node (recall cgroups and QoS).
The app still needs somewhere to write temporary files, so mount an emptyDir (a scratch volume that starts empty and is deleted with the pod) at /tmp. Writable space is now explicit.

blocks.md: How do you know the before version is weak without reading it line by line? The API server can tell you. Pod Security Admission (lesson 10) checks pods against the **Restricted** profile and, in warn mode, prints exactly what is missing. This is the output the Kubernetes tutorial shows for a basic nginx pod:

blocks.code:
Warning: would violate PodSecurity "restricted:latest": allowPrivilegeEscalation != false (container "nginx" must set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false), unrestricted capabilities (container "nginx" must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"]), runAsNonRoot != true (pod or container "nginx" must set securityContext.runAsNonRoot=true), seccompProfile (pod or container "nginx" must set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost")
pod/nginx created
blocks.caption: From the Kubernetes tutorial on namespace-level Pod Security Standards. The four items are exactly lines 10, 13-14, 19 and 21-22 of the hardened spec.

blocks.prompt: You apply the hardened spec, and the pod crashes on start with "read-only file system" while writing to `/var/cache/app`. What is the right fix?
blocks.reveal: Mount another `emptyDir` at `/var/cache/app`, or configure the app to use `/tmp`. Do not drop `readOnlyRootFilesystem`. The error is the setting doing its job: it found a path the app writes to that you had not declared. Each writable path should be a deliberate, named volume.

blocks.md: Misconception: "runAsNonRoot is enough". It stops UID 0, but a non-root process with `allowPrivilegeEscalation` left at its default of true can still become root through a setuid binary in the image. Set both, and drop capabilities.

Hardened default for application pods: no token, non-root, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no privilege escalation, read-only root filesystem, drop ALL capabilities, explicit writable volumes, resource limits, image by digest.

blocks.question: A pod sets `runAsNonRoot: true` and nothing else in its security context. Its image contains a setuid-root helper. Which missing setting would block the helper from raising privileges?
blocks.explain: no_new_privs makes the kernel ignore the setuid bit on exec. allowPrivilegeEscalation defaults to true, so it must be set explicitly to false.

blocks.question: Your cluster's kubelets run without seccompDefault. A pod spec sets no seccompProfile. Which seccomp profile does it get?
blocks.explain: The Kubernetes seccomp tutorial says pods use RuntimeDefault by default only when seccompDefault is enabled; otherwise the default is Unconfined. Set it in the pod or enable the kubelet option.

lessons.title: The API server is the front door: authn, authz, admission

blocks.md:
**Kubernetes** (from the Greek for helmsman or pilot, per its documentation; "K8s" counts the eight letters between K and s) is a set of programs that run containers across many machines. For security, one fact organises everything: **every change goes through the API server**. Whoever can talk to it with enough rights controls the cluster.

The [components](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/components/) from a defender's view:

- **kube-apiserver**: the HTTP API in front of all cluster state. Port 6443.
- **etcd**: the store for all API data, every Secret included (per [etcd's docs](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/learning/why/), the name joins Unix's `/etc` configuration folder and "d" for distributed). Ports 2379-2380.
- **kubelet**: the agent on every node that starts containers, with its own HTTPS API on port 10250 (lesson 13).
- **kube-scheduler** and **kube-controller-manager**: control loops that work through the API server.

Hence the checklist rule: the API server, kubelet API and etcd should not be exposed on the internet.

The [access control overview](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/controlling-access/) describes what happens to each request, in order:

1. **Transport**: TLS (Transport Layer Security) protects the connection.
2. **Authentication** (authn: "who are you?"). Modules such as client certificates, bearer tokens and service account tokens (JSON Web Tokens, JWTs) are tried in turn. If none succeeds the request is rejected with **401**.
3. **Authorization** (authz: "may you do this?"). Modules such as RBAC (role-based access control) and Webhook are consulted; if any allows, it proceeds; if all deny, **403**.
4. **Admission control**. Modules that can **modify** (mutating) or **reject** (validating) the object being created or changed. Mutating runs first, then validating. Unlike authorization, if any admission controller rejects, the request is rejected immediately.
5. **Persist** to etcd.

One detail with big consequences: per the [admission controllers page](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/admission-controllers/), admission controllers act on create, update, delete and connect, but "do not (and cannot) block requests to read (get, watch or list) objects". Only authorization guards reads.

blocks.title: One API request through authentication, authorization and admission

scenes.caption: alice runs kubectl apply. The request arrives over TLS with a bearer token. Authentication modules try to identify it.
Authorization asks: may alice create pods in namespace shop? RBAC finds a RoleBinding that allows it.
Admission sees the full object. Mutating controllers run first (for example, set defaults); then validating ones (for example, Pod Security, policy webhooks).
All passed. The object is validated against its schema and written to etcd. Only now do the scheduler and kubelet act on it.
A request with an expired or unknown token: no authenticator accepts it, so it stops at step 1 with 401.
bob is authenticated but asks to delete Secrets in shop. No rule allows it, so authorization answers 403.
alice tries a privileged pod in a namespace enforcing the Restricted profile. RBAC allows pod creation, but the Pod Security admission controller rejects the object.
A read: list Secrets. Reads skip admission entirely. If RBAC allows it, every Secret's contents come back. Authorization is the only gate on reads.

blocks.md: How do you check what an identity may do without trying it? `kubectl auth can-i` asks the authorization layer through the SelfSubjectAccessReview API and "works regardless of the authorization mode used", per the [authorization docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authorization/). Administrators can add `--as` to impersonate another user or a service account.

blocks.code:
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --namespace dev
yes
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --namespace prod
no
kubectl auth can-i list secrets --namespace dev --as dave
no
kubectl auth can-i list pods --namespace target --as system:serviceaccount:dev:dev-sa
yes
blocks.caption: Each command is followed by its output, as the Kubernetes authorization page shows them. The output is just yes or no; add --list to print every allowed action in a namespace.

blocks.md:
**Defender view: the audit log.** [Auditing](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug/debug-cluster/audit/) records each request in stages (RequestReceived, ResponseStarted for long-running requests, ResponseComplete, Panic) at a level set by an audit policy: `None`, `Metadata` (who, when, which resource and verb), `Request` (plus the request body) or `RequestResponse` (plus the response body). It answers who did what, to which object, from where.

Two warnings from the docs. If the `--audit-policy-file` flag is omitted, **no events are logged**. And logging Secrets at `Request` or `RequestResponse` writes their values into the log, so policies typically log Secrets at `Metadata` only, as the documentation's example policy does.

Every request passes authentication (401 if unknown), authorization (403 if not allowed), then admission (mutate, then validate) before etcd. Reads skip admission, so RBAC alone protects them. Turn on audit logging, because it is off unless you configure it.

blocks.question: A policy engine in admission rejects any pod that mounts a Secret. Can a user who has `list` on Secrets in that namespace still read every Secret's value?
options: Only if audit logging is off
Yes: list is a read, reads skip admission, and the list response includes Secret contents
blocks.explain: Admission only sees create, update, delete and connect. Reads are decided by authorization alone, and the RBAC good-practices page notes list and watch on Secrets reveal their contents.

blocks.question: A request returns 403 Forbidden with the message `User "bob" cannot delete resource "secrets" in API group "" in the namespace "shop"`. Which step rejected it?
options: Authorization: the identity is known but no policy allows the action
blocks.explain: 401 means no authenticator recognised the request. This message names a known user and a missing permission: every authorization module denied it. Read the message, not only the code: admission rejections such as Pod Security are also 403 Forbidden, but their message names the policy ("violates PodSecurity").

lessons.title: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate

blocks.md:
**RBAC** (role-based access control: rights are attached to roles, and people or programs get roles) is the authorization module almost every cluster uses. The [RBAC docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac/) define four objects:

- **Role**: a list of rules (API groups, resources, verbs) valid inside **one namespace**.
- **ClusterRole**: the same, but not namespaced, so it can cover cluster-wide resources such as nodes, or be reused in many namespaces.
- **RoleBinding**: grants a Role or ClusterRole to subjects (users, groups, service accounts) **within the binding's namespace**.
- **ClusterRoleBinding**: grants a ClusterRole across the **whole cluster**.

"Permissions are purely additive (there are no deny rules)." You cannot subtract a right; you can only avoid granting it.

blocks.title: How a binding connects who to what

scenes.caption: A tiny cluster. jane is a developer; ci-deployer is the service account a CI pipeline uses. Two roles exist.
A RoleBinding in namespace shop grants jane the Role pod-reader: get, watch, list on pods, only in shop.
Someone "fixes" a failing deploy by binding ci-deployer to cluster-admin with a ClusterRoleBinding. Now CI holds every verb on every resource in every namespace.
Least privilege: a Role allowing get and patch on the one Deployment CI updates, bound by a RoleBinding in shop. A stolen CI token now changes one Deployment, not the cluster.

blocks.code:
# Too broad: CI can do anything, anywhere
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: ci-deployer-admin
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: ci-deployer
  namespace: ci
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: cluster-admin
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
# Also too broad: wildcards match every resource, including ones added later
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: everything
rules:
- apiGroups: ["*"]
  resources: ["*"]
  verbs: ["*"]
blocks.caption: Before. The RBAC good-practices page warns that wildcards grant rights to all object types that exist now and to any created in the future.

blocks.code:
# Least privilege: patch one Deployment in one namespace
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: deploy-web
  namespace: shop
rules:
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  resourceNames: ["web"]
  verbs: ["get", "patch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: ci-deployer-web
  namespace: shop
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: ci-deployer
  namespace: ci
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: deploy-web
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
blocks.caption: After. Check it: kubectl auth can-i patch deployments/web -n shop --as system:serviceaccount:ci:ci-deployer should print yes, and the same question for list secrets should print no.

blocks.md:
Some permissions look small and are not. The [RBAC good practices](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/rbac-good-practices/) page lists escalation risks:

- **list or watch on Secrets** reveal contents, not just names; `kubectl get secrets -A -o yaml` returns every value.
- **create pods** (or Deployments, Jobs and so on) in a namespace implicitly grants the Secrets, ConfigMaps and volumes the pod can mount, and the rights of **any service account** in that namespace, since a pod can run as any of them.
- **get on `nodes/proxy`** reaches the kubelet API, which "allows for command execution on every pod on the node", and "bypasses audit logging and admission control".
- **escalate**, **bind** and **impersonate** verbs let a user create roles or bindings beyond their own rights, or act as someone else.
- **create on `serviceaccounts/token`** issues tokens for existing service accounts.
- Membership of **`system:masters`** bypasses RBAC entirely and cannot be revoked by removing bindings; the security checklist says to use it only as break-glass.

Misconception: "they can only create pods, not read Secrets". Pod creation lets them mount any Secret in the namespace into a pod they control and read it from inside. Treat create-pods as read-all-secrets for that namespace, unless admission policy restricts what pods may mount.

Defender view. Prevent: RoleBindings over ClusterRoleBindings, no wildcards, no cluster-admin for automation. Detect: audit-log alerts on new ClusterRoleBindings, bindings to cluster-admin, use of impersonation, and list on Secrets by unusual identities. Review: run `kubectl auth can-i --list` as each service account periodically; the checklist suggests access reviews at least every 24 months.
RBAC only adds. Grant namespaced Roles with explicit resources, names and verbs. Treat Secrets list, pod creation, nodes/proxy, escalate, bind and impersonate as administrator-level rights.

blocks.question: A RoleBinding in namespace dev references the ClusterRole secret-reader. Where can the subject read Secrets?
options: In every namespace, because it is a ClusterRole
Only in dev, because a RoleBinding grants within its own namespace
blocks.explain: The RBAC docs give this exact example: a RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole, and the binding's namespace decides where the rights apply. Only a ClusterRoleBinding grants cluster-wide.

blocks.question: Which grant gives a user the ability to run commands in any pod on a node, without appearing in the API audit log as pod exec?
blocks.explain: nodes/proxy reaches the kubelet API, including exec. The good-practices page says it bypasses audit logging and admission control, and that even the get verb is enough because websocket requests are authorized as get.

blocks.question: You must stop one compromised user immediately. They are a member of system:masters. What works?
options: Add a deny rule for them
Revoke their credential (for example the client certificate) at the authentication layer, because system:masters bypasses RBAC
blocks.explain: system:masters skips RBAC, so bindings are irrelevant, and RBAC has no deny rules. The fix is at authentication. The authentication docs state Kubernetes does not support certificate revocation, so for a client certificate this can mean rotating the signing CA.

lessons.title: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods

blocks.md:
Programs inside pods need identities too. In Kubernetes that identity is a **ServiceAccount**: an API object whose credentials the pod uses to call the API server. It authenticates with the username `system:serviceaccount:NAMESPACE:NAME`, and belongs to the groups `system:serviceaccounts` and `system:serviceaccounts:NAMESPACE`, per the [authentication docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication/).

Every namespace automatically has one named `default`, and a pod that names no service account runs as it. The [service accounts page](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/service-accounts/) says default service accounts get no permissions beyond API discovery when RBAC is on. That stays true only until someone binds a role to `default` to make one app work, at which point every pod in the namespace inherits it.

How does the pod get its credential? By default the kubelet requests a **short-lived, automatically rotating token** through the TokenRequest API and mounts it as a projected volume at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`. The token is a **JWT** (JSON Web Token: a signed, base64url-encoded JSON document stating who it was issued to, for which audience, and until when).

History matters when you audit old clusters: before Kubernetes 1.24, a **permanent** token was created automatically for each service account and stored in a Secret. Such tokens "don't expire and don't rotate". They can still be created by hand, and the docs recommend against it.

Anyone who can read that file, for example through a path traversal bug in the app, holds the pod's API identity. If the app never calls the Kubernetes API, the token is pure risk.

blocks.code:
# Opt out on the service account: pods using it get no token by default
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
# Or per pod; the pod spec setting takes precedence over the service account
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  serviceAccountName: web
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: registry.example.com/shop/web@sha256:<digest>
blocks.caption: Both forms appear in the Kubernetes docs. Give each app its own service account rather than sharing default, so a binding meant for one app does not leak to all.

blocks.md:
**Cloud identity.** Pods often need cloud APIs too: read a storage bucket, write to a queue. Recall from the server-side web attacks course that every cloud VM can fetch temporary credentials for its attached IAM role from the **instance metadata service** (IMDS) at the link-local address 169.254.169.254. On a Kubernetes node, every pod is on that VM. AWS's EKS documentation says that if IMDS is not restricted, a pod's containers "also have access to the Amazon EKS node IAM role" and possibly other pods' roles. One foothold in any pod then reaches the node's cloud role.

The fix is **workload identity**: map a Kubernetes service account to a cloud role, so each pod gets only its own role's short-lived credentials. On AWS this is IRSA ([IAM roles for service accounts](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/iam-roles-for-service-accounts.html)) or the newer EKS Pod Identity; on Google Cloud it is [Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity); Azure has its own equivalent.

blocks.title: IRSA: trading a Kubernetes token for scoped AWS credentials

scenes.caption: An EKS webhook sees pods whose service account carries the IAM role annotation and adds a token file mount and AWS settings to them. The kubelet asks the API server for that projected token.
The kubelet mounts the token into the pod as a file and refreshes it before it expires.
The AWS SDK in the pod sends the token to AWS STS (Security Token Service) with AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. STS checks the signature against the cluster's public OIDC keys, which EKS publishes.
STS returns temporary credentials for exactly the role mapped to this service account, nothing else.
The pod reads the one bucket its role allows. Calls are logged in CloudTrail under that role, so the audit trail names the workload, not the node.
An attacker in this pod who tries another bucket is refused. The blast radius is one role, provided the node's metadata endpoint is also blocked for pods.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/web-reader
blocks.caption: The IRSA annotation format from AWS's documentation. The IAM role's trust policy must also restrict which namespace and service account may assume it, or any pod with a valid cluster token could.

blocks.md: AWS states it plainly: "Containers are not a security boundary, and the use of IAM roles for service accounts does not change this." Workload identity scopes credentials per pod, but an escaped container can act as anything on the node. Also, pods with hostNetwork: true always reach IMDS.

Defender view. Prevent: automount off by default, one service account per app, workload identity instead of node roles or static keys, and block pod access to the metadata address (AWS's EKS best practices guide does this by requiring IMDSv2 with a response hop limit of 1). Detect: CloudTrail calls made with the node role from unexpected sources; Kubernetes audit events for TokenRequest on service accounts by unusual users.

A pod's identity is its service account token plus whatever cloud role it can reach. Mount tokens only where needed, give each app its own service account, and map cloud access per service account instead of per node.

blocks.question: Five apps in namespace shop all use the default service account. An admin binds a Role allowing `get secrets` to it so one app can read its config. What changed for the other four?
options: All four can now read Secrets in shop, because they run as the same identity
Only if they mount the Secret
Only pods created after the binding are affected
blocks.explain: RBAC grants rights to the identity, and all five pods share it. Give each app its own service account so a binding affects only the app that needs it.

blocks.question: A cluster on AWS uses IRSA for every app, but pods can still reach the instance metadata service. What can an attacker in any pod do?
options: Fetch the node's IAM role credentials from IMDS and act with the node role's permissions
Only read their own role's credentials
blocks.explain: AWS's docs say containers have access to the node IAM role when IMDS is not restricted. IRSA adds a better path; it does not close the old one. Block or limit IMDS for pods too.

lessons.title: Pod Security Admission and policy engines

blocks.md:
Lessons 5 and 6 listed settings to forbid and settings to require. Writing them down is not enough; someone will ship a chart with `privileged: true` on a Friday. **Admission control** (lesson 7) is where the cluster says no.

The Kubernetes project publishes three named profiles, the [Pod Security Standards](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/):

- **Privileged**: "Unrestricted policy... allows for known privilege escalations." For trusted system workloads only.
- **Baseline**: "prevents known privilege escalations" while allowing the default pod. Forbids host namespaces, privileged containers, hostPath volumes, host ports, extra capabilities beyond a short allowed list, and Unconfined seccomp; restricts AppArmor, SELinux, /proc mount type and sysctls.
- **Restricted**: everything in Baseline, plus only safe volume types, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `runAsNonRoot: true`, no `runAsUser` of 0, seccomp `RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost` set explicitly, and capabilities drop `ALL` (only `NET_BIND_SERVICE` may be added back).

The built-in enforcer is **Pod Security Admission** (PSA), stable since Kubernetes 1.25. It replaced PodSecurityPolicy, which was deprecated in 1.21 and removed in 1.25. You configure it per namespace with labels. Each label pairs a **mode** with a **level**:

- `enforce`: violations are rejected.
- `audit`: violations are allowed but annotated in the audit log.
- `warn`: violations are allowed but the user sees a warning.

A namespace can use all three, at different levels. A common rollout is `enforce: baseline` with `warn` and `audit` at `restricted`, so teams see what will break before you tighten.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version: latest
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version: latest
blocks.caption: The label scheme from the Pod Security Admission docs. The -version labels pin a level to the rules of a given Kubernetes minor version, or latest.

blocks.title: What Pod Security Admission does with three different requests

nodes.label:
PSA: shop
enforce baseline
warn restricted

scenes.caption: Namespace shop enforces Baseline and warns at Restricted. Three requests arrive at the API server's admission stage.
A pod with a hostPath volume violates Baseline. enforce rejects it; nothing is stored, nothing runs.
A pod with no securityContext passes Baseline but not Restricted. It is admitted, and kubectl prints a "would violate PodSecurity" warning listing the missing fields.
A Deployment whose template adds hostPath. The docs say enforce applies only to pods, not workload objects, so the Deployment is accepted (audit and warn do flag it).
Its ReplicaSet then tries to create pods, and every pod is rejected. The Deployment exists but never runs; the error appears in the ReplicaSet's events, not in your kubectl output.

blocks.md:
PSA is deliberately simple: three fixed levels, per namespace. For anything else, such as "images must come from our registry", "every pod needs resource limits", or "images must be signed" (lesson 4), clusters add a **policy engine** that runs as an admission webhook:

- [Kyverno](https://kyverno.io/docs/introduction/) ("Greek for govern", in its own words) writes policies as Kubernetes YAML and can validate, mutate, generate and verify images.
- [OPA Gatekeeper](https://open-policy-agent.github.io/gatekeeper/website/docs/) runs policies in Rego, the language of OPA (Open Policy Agent, a general policy engine and graduated project of the CNCF, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation), defined through ConstraintTemplate and Constraint objects. Its audit function reports objects that already violate a policy.

Kubernetes itself now has **ValidatingAdmissionPolicy**, which expresses checks in CEL (Common Expression Language) inside the API server without a webhook.

Webhooks bring their own risks, and both are about the webhook being a separate service:

- **Failure mode.** Each webhook has a `failurePolicy`: `Fail` (the default) rejects requests when the webhook cannot be reached, `Ignore` lets them through. A security policy set to `Ignore` can be bypassed by making its webhook unavailable; a `Fail` policy can block all deploys if its pods crash.
- **The webhook is an attack surface.** It is an HTTPS server inside the cluster that receives whole objects, often with powerful rights. Lesson 11 shows what happened when one could be reached from any pod: IngressNightmare.

Misconception: "we enforce Restricted, so pods are safe". PSA checks pod fields only. It does not check the image, RBAC, network policy or which Secrets are mounted, and namespaces or users can be exempted in its configuration. It is one layer.

Label every namespace with a Pod Security level: Restricted for applications, Baseline at minimum, Privileged only for reviewed system namespaces. Add a policy engine for rules PSA cannot express, and treat its webhook as critical infrastructure.

blocks.question: A namespace has `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`. A user applies a Deployment whose pod template sets `privileged: true`. What happens?
options: The Deployment is accepted, but its pods are rejected when the ReplicaSet tries to create them
PSA mutates the template to remove privileged
The pods start but are killed after 60 seconds
blocks.explain: The PSA docs state enforce applies only to the resulting pod objects, while audit and warn also apply to workload resources. PSA validates; it never mutates.

blocks.question: A security webhook is configured with `failurePolicy: Ignore`. An attacker who can create pods also manages to crash the webhook's pods. What is the effect?
options: Pods are admitted without that webhook's checks while it is down
The API server restarts the webhook
blocks.explain: Ignore means the API server skips the webhook when it cannot be called. For a security control, Fail is usually right, with the webhook run highly available.

lessons.title: Network policies: from default allow to default deny

blocks.md:
Here is the default that surprises most people: in Kubernetes, **every pod can connect to every other pod**, across all namespaces. The [Network Policies page](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/) says "By default, a pod is non-isolated for egress; all outbound connections are allowed" and the same for ingress. A foothold in the least important pod is one TCP connection from your database.

A **NetworkPolicy** is a namespaced object that controls traffic at the IP address and port level (layers 3 and 4: IP addresses, and TCP, UDP or SCTP ports). It needs a network plugin that implements it: the docs warn that creating one "without a controller that implements it will have no effect". Plugins follow the CNI (Container Network Interface) standard; some enforce policies and some do not.

The rules, from the documentation:

1. A pod becomes **isolated** for ingress (or egress) as soon as any policy that selects it lists Ingress (or Egress) in `policyTypes`. Until then, everything is allowed in that direction.
2. Once isolated, only connections that some selecting policy allows get through. Reply traffic for an allowed connection is allowed automatically.
3. Policies are **additive**: the allowed set is the union of all policies selecting the pod. There are no deny rules and no ordering.
4. A connection needs **both** sides to allow it: egress on the source pod and ingress on the destination pod.
5. Exceptions: a pod cannot block traffic to itself, and traffic to and from the pod's own node is always allowed.

So "default deny" is simply a policy that selects every pod (`podSelector: {}`) and allows nothing. Then you add narrow allow policies.

blocks.title: Who can connect to whom in namespace shop (1 = allowed)

scenes.caption: Default: no policies, so every source (row) reaches every destination (column). The debug pod, where an attacker landed, can reach the database directly.
Apply default-deny-all (Ingress and Egress, podSelector {}). Everything is blocked except a pod talking to itself, which a policy cannot block.
Allow frontend to api on TCP 8080: an egress rule on frontend and an ingress rule on api. Both sides must allow.
Allow api to db on the database port the same way. This is the whole intended traffic graph.
The attacker in debug now reaches nothing. To get to db they must first compromise frontend, then api: two more bugs instead of zero.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
---
# Default-deny egress also blocks DNS, so allow lookups to the cluster DNS pods
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
blocks.caption: The first policy is the documentation's default-deny-all. The docs warn that it also blocks DNS. kubernetes.io/metadata.name is a label the control plane sets on every namespace; k8s-app: kube-dns is the usual label on cluster DNS pods (check yours).

blocks.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-ingress-from-frontend
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: frontend-egress-to-api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: api
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
blocks.caption: One allowed edge needs both halves once both pods are isolated: ingress on the destination, egress on the source.

blocks.md:
**Real case: IngressNightmare (CVE-2025-1974), March 2025.** An **Ingress** (from the English word for entry) is the Kubernetes object that describes how outside HTTP traffic reaches services; an ingress controller turns it into proxy configuration. ingress-nginx, the project's own NGINX-based controller, was in "over 40%" of clusters per the [Kubernetes blog](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/03/24/ingress-nginx-cve-2025-1974/).

Researchers at Wiz, a cloud security company (Nir Ohfeld, Sagi Tzadik, Ronen Shustin, Hillai Ben-Sasson), found that its validating admission webhook, which builds a test NGINX configuration from each submitted Ingress, could be fed configuration that loaded attacker code. The webhook was reachable over the network **without authentication**, and ingress-nginx can by default read all Secrets cluster-wide, so the blog warns "anything on the Pod network has a good chance of taking over your Kubernetes cluster". CVSS score 9.8. [Wiz](https://www.wiz.io/blog/ingress-nginx-kubernetes-vulnerabilities) found over 6,500 clusters exposing the webhook to the internet.

The fixes were ingress-nginx v1.12.1 and v1.11.5. As interim mitigations, Wiz advised "Enforce strict network policies so only the Kubernetes API Server can access the admission controller", or turning the webhook off until upgraded. That is this lesson in one sentence: under default allow, an internal admin endpoint is an endpoint for every compromised pod.

Currency note: ingress-nginx itself has since been retired. The [Kubernetes blog](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/11/11/ingress-nginx-retirement/) announced that maintenance would stop in March 2026, after which there are "no further releases, no bugfixes, and no updates to resolve any security vulnerabilities". Existing installs keep running but will not be patched again, so the project recommends migrating to Gateway API, the newer Kubernetes routing API, or to another ingress controller.
Misconception: "the database is internal, so it is not exposed". Internal means reachable by every pod in the cluster unless a policy says otherwise. Treat the pod network as a hostile network.

Defender view. Prevent: confirm your CNI enforces policies, then default-deny ingress and egress in every namespace, with explicit allows including DNS and the API server for pods that need it. Detect: plugins that log denied flows give a signal when a pod probes neighbours; unexpected egress to the internet from a backend pod is a classic sign of mining or exfiltration. Also block pod egress to the cloud metadata address unless needed.
Pods are non-isolated until a policy selects them. Start each namespace with default deny for both directions, add DNS, then add one allow per intended connection, on both sides.

blocks.question: Namespace shop has only one NetworkPolicy: it selects `app: db` and allows ingress from `app: api`. Can the `frontend` pod open a connection to the `debug` pod?
options: Yes: only db pods are selected by a policy, so frontend and debug remain non-isolated
No, because policies are evaluated in order
No, the namespace is now isolated
blocks.explain: Isolation is per pod. A pod no policy selects stays fully open. That is why a namespace-wide default deny with podSelector {} is the starting point.

blocks.question: After applying default-deny-all, every app fails with name resolution errors, but the allow rules between apps look right. What is missing?
options: An ingress rule on the DNS pods
An egress rule allowing UDP and TCP port 53 to the cluster DNS pods
blocks.explain: Default deny for egress also blocks DNS queries, as the docs warn. Add an egress allow to the cluster DNS service on port 53.

blocks.md: A Kubernetes **Secret** is an object for small confidential values: passwords, API tokens, TLS keys. Open one and the values look scrambled. They are not. They are **base64**, an encoding that turns any bytes into 64 printable characters so binary data fits in YAML and JSON. Encoding is reversible by anyone; encryption needs a key. The Kubernetes docs say it outright in their TLS Secret example: values are base64 encoded, "which obscures them but does NOT provide" confidentiality.

blocks.title: Base64 maps every 3 bytes to 4 characters, with no key

scenes.caption: The secret value p4ssw0rd, 8 bytes. Base64 works on groups of 3 bytes (24 bits), splitting each group into four 6-bit numbers, each picking one of 64 characters.
Bytes p, 4, s become cDRz. Same input, same output, every time, on every machine.
Bytes s, w, 0 become c3cw.
The last two bytes r, d become cmQ and one = pad character, because the final group had only 2 bytes.
Reversing it needs no secret at all: base64 -d gives p4ssw0rd back. Anyone who can read the object can read the password.

blocks.code:
kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password=p4ssw0rd
secret/db created
kubectl get secret db -o jsonpath='{.data.password}'
cDRzc3cwcmQ=
echo 'cDRzc3cwcmQ=' | base64 -d
p4ssw0rd
blocks.caption: Each command is followed by its output. Anyone with get on this Secret, or list on Secrets in the namespace, can do this. The base64 values were computed with a script.

blocks.md:
Where do Secrets live? In etcd, with every other object. The [Secrets page](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/) warns that they are "by default, stored unencrypted in the API server's underlying data store (etcd). Anyone with API access can retrieve or modify a Secret, and so can anyone with access to etcd." So an etcd backup file, a stolen etcd disk snapshot, or network access to etcd's port without client certificates is a copy of every credential in the cluster.

The docs add the indirect path from lesson 8: "anyone who is authorized to create a Pod in a namespace can use that access to read any Secret in that namespace".

**Encryption at rest** makes the API server encrypt resources before writing them to etcd. It is configured with an `EncryptionConfiguration` file passed via `--encryption-provider-config`. The [encryption guide](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/encrypt-data/) lists providers in order of preference. Key points:

- Providers are an **ordered list**. The first encrypts new writes; all are tried for reading. If `identity` (no encryption) is first, nothing is encrypted.
- Local-key providers (`aescbc`, `aesgcm`, `secretbox`) keep the key in a file on the control plane host, next to the data it protects. The docs mark `aescbc` "Not recommended due to CBC's vulnerability to padding oracle attacks."
- **KMS v2** (KMS: key management service, an external service that holds keys and encrypts with them) uses **envelope encryption**: each value is encrypted with a data encryption key (DEK), and DEKs are protected by a key encryption key (KEK) held in that external service. The KEK never sits in the cluster.
- Existing Secrets stay as they were until rewritten.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources:
      - secrets
    providers:
      - kms:
          apiVersion: v2
          name: myKmsPlugin
          endpoint: unix:///tmp/socketfile.sock
      - identity: {}   # fallback so existing plaintext data can still be read
blocks.caption: KMS v2 first, so all new writes are envelope-encrypted; identity last only so data written before the change stays readable. After restarting the API servers, the docs say to rewrite every Secret: kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -

The encryption guide reads a Secret straight from etcd with etcdctl (etcd's command-line client) and hexdump (prints bytes as hex). The k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:key1: prefix, then random-looking bytes, proves encryption. Abbreviated from the docs (aescbc); with KMS v2 the prefix is k8s:enc:kms:v2:

blocks.md: Encryption at rest protects against stolen disks and backups. It does **not** protect against anyone the API server serves the Secret to, because it decrypts on read. Access control still matters most. The [Secrets good practices](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/secrets-good-practices/) page adds: restrict get, list and watch to the components that need them, only cluster admins may touch etcd, and consider keeping values outside the cluster with an **external secret store** (a vault service from your cloud or a dedicated product). The Kubernetes **Secrets Store CSI Driver** (CSI: Container Storage Interface, the plugin standard for volumes) lets the kubelet fetch values from such a store and mount them only into authorized pods.

Misconception: "our Secrets are encrypted because they look scrambled in kubectl". That is base64. Check whether the API server has --encryption-provider-config at all, and whether identity is first; the docs list both as signs that encryption at rest is not enabled.

base64 hides nothing. Lock down who can get, list or watch Secrets and who can create pods, encrypt etcd data with a KMS provider, rewrite existing Secrets after enabling it, and keep high-value credentials in an external store.

blocks.question: An EncryptionConfiguration lists providers in the order identity, aesgcm. New Secrets are written. Are they encrypted in etcd?
options: No: the first provider encrypts new writes, and identity means plain text
blocks.explain: The guide says if identity is the first provider, at-rest encryption is not enabled. The second provider is only tried when reading data it previously wrote.

blocks.question: Encryption at rest with KMS v2 is enabled. A developer has `list secrets` in namespace shop. What does encryption at rest change for them?
options: Nothing: the API server decrypts on read, so authorized readers see plain values
blocks.explain: Encryption at rest protects etcd's stored data and backups. Anyone the API server authorizes still gets the decrypted value, which is why RBAC on Secrets is the main control.

lessons.title: Exposed dashboards, kubelets and Docker APIs

blocks.md:
Most real container incidents involve no clever exploit at all. Someone left a management interface reachable without a password, and someone else found it with an internet scan. Attackers rarely steal data in these cases; they run **cryptocurrency miners**, mostly for Monero (a cryptocurrency whose RandomX mining algorithm is optimised for ordinary CPUs), because stolen compute converts straight into money. This is called **cryptojacking**: using someone else's computers to mine without permission.

Three interfaces keep showing up: the Kubernetes Dashboard (a web UI for the cluster), the kubelet API on every node, and the Docker daemon's API.

**Real case: Tesla, 2018.** On February 20, 2018 the RedLock Cloud Security Intelligence team (RedLock was a cloud security company, now part of Palo Alto Networks) [reported](https://web.archive.org/web/2018/https://redlock.io/blog/cryptojacking-tesla) that "hackers had infiltrated Tesla's Kubernetes console which was not password protected. Within one Kubernetes pod, access credentials were exposed to Tesla's AWS environment", which held an S3 bucket with sensitive data such as telemetry. The attackers also ran mining software in a pod.

The evasion was the interesting part: an unlisted mining pool instead of a public one, its IP address hidden behind the Cloudflare content delivery network, a non-standard port, and low CPU usage. Each trick defeats one simple detector: blocklists, IP reputation, port rules, CPU alarms. RedLock reported it and Tesla fixed it quickly. Months earlier the team had found hundreds of such open consoles, including at Aviva and Gemalto.
