blocks.title: The Tesla chain: one open console to a cloud account

scenes.caption: The pieces: an internet-facing Kubernetes console, a pod with AWS credentials in its configuration, the AWS account behind them.
Step 1: the console answers anyone who finds it. No password is required.
Step 2: through the console the attacker finds AWS access credentials exposed in one pod.
Step 3: those keys reach the AWS account, including an S3 bucket with telemetry. A cluster problem is now a cloud data problem.
Step 4: the attacker starts miners in a pod, connecting to an unlisted pool behind Cloudflare on a non-standard port, throttled to low CPU.
Breaks in the chain: never expose the console; give it minimal rights and require login; keep cloud keys out of pod configs (workload identity, lesson 9); restrict egress (lesson 11).

blocks.md:
The Dashboard today: the [Kubernetes docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/access-application-cluster/web-ui-dashboard/) mark it "deprecated and unmaintained" and suggest Headlamp, another web UI for Kubernetes. Recent versions deploy with "a minimal RBAC configuration by default" and accept only bearer token login. For any UI: not on the internet, login required, least-privilege service account.

**The kubelet API** (port 10250) can list pods, read logs and run commands in containers. The [kubelet auth docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/kubelet-authn-authz/) say unauthenticated requests become `system:anonymous` by default, and "The default authorization mode is AlwaysAllow". Those are the command-line defaults; the configuration file's defaults are safe (anonymous off, Webhook). The checklist warns the defaults with no `--config` file "are overly permissive". Managed services set this correctly; hand-built clusters often did not.

blocks.title: TeamTNT's Hildegard campaign through anonymous kubelets

scenes.caption: Initial access, per Unit 42: the attacker sends a command to a kubelet that allows anonymous access, using its run-command API on a container.
The command starts tmate, a terminal sharing tool, as a reverse shell: the container connects out to the attacker, so no inbound port is needed.
From inside, the attacker scans the cluster's internal network with masscan, a fast port scanner, and finds more open kubelets on other nodes.
Containers on those nodes get a mining script that runs xmrig, a Monero miner, and reports to an IRC (Internet Relay Chat) channel used for command and control.
Hiding: a library listed in /etc/ld.so.preload is loaded into every program and filters /proc listings, so ps and top inside the container do not show the miner.
The fix at step 1: anonymous auth off and Webhook authorization. The same request now gets 401 and nothing after it happens.

blocks.md: **Real case: TeamTNT and Hildegard, 2021.** Unit 42, the threat research team at Palo Alto Networks (researchers Aviv Sasson and Ariel Zelivansky), [published](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hildegard-malware-teamtnt/) on February 3, 2021 a campaign it named Hildegard, after the username of the tmate account it used. It attributed it to TeamTNT, a group "known for exploiting unsecured Docker daemons and deploying malicious container images", and noted this was the first time it had seen TeamTNT target Kubernetes. The malware also dropped Peirates and BOtB, tools that look for cloud credentials and service account tokens and try known container escapes such as CVE-2019-5736 (lesson 14).

**Exposed Docker APIs.** Docker's daemon can listen on TCP; by convention port 2375 is unencrypted and 2376 is TLS. Unit 42's earlier [Graboid](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/graboid-first-ever-cryptojacking-worm-found-in-images-on-docker-hub/) report (October 2019) found a cryptojacking worm that had spread to more than 2,000 unsecured Docker hosts: "Without any authentication or authorization, a malicious actor can take full control of the Docker Engine (CE) and the host." Docker's [security docs](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/) now say exposing the API over HTTP without TLS is not permitted and makes the daemon fail at startup.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false          # unauthenticated requests get 401
  webhook:
    enabled: true           # validate bearer tokens with the API server (TokenReview)
  x509:
    clientCAFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
authorization:
  mode: Webhook             # ask the API server (SubjectAccessReview), not AlwaysAllow
readOnlyPort: 0             # the unauthenticated read-only port stays disabled
blocks.caption: Field names from the kubelet configuration reference. Apart from the CA file path, which has no default, these values are also that file format's defaults; writing them explicitly documents intent and survives someone adding command-line flags.

blocks.md: Defender view. Prevent: no management API on the internet; kubelet anonymous auth off with Webhook authorization; Docker only on its Unix socket or mutual TLS. Detect: scan your own address ranges for ports 2375, 2376, 6443, 10250 and 2379; enable Falco's miner rules (sandbox maturity, some off by default); watch fleet-wide billing and CPU, not just per pod. Respond: assume every credential reachable from the exposed surface was taken, and rotate it.

Exposed management APIs are the most common real container compromise, and the usual payoff is mining. Every API that can start or exec into containers must require authentication and sit off the internet.

blocks.question: A self-built cluster's kubelets run with flags only, no config file, and `--anonymous-auth` and `--authorization-mode` are not set. Port 10250 is reachable from the internet. What can an unauthenticated stranger do?
options: Run commands in containers through the kubelet API, since anonymous requests are allowed and authorization defaults to AlwaysAllow
blocks.explain: The kubelet auth docs give these defaults: anonymous requests accepted, AlwaysAllow authorization. TLS encrypts the connection but does not authenticate the caller. This is the Hildegard entry point.

blocks.question: Tesla's attackers kept CPU usage low and used an unlisted pool behind a CDN on a non-standard port. Which detection was hardest for them to evade?
options: A port-based firewall rule for well-known mining ports
A process-level rule that flags known miner binaries or mining protocol command lines, combined with egress allowlists
A blocklist of known mining pool domains
blocks.explain: Each listed evasion targets one simple signal: domain lists, IP reputation, port rules, CPU alarms. Watching what processes run and allowing only expected outbound connections does not depend on those surface features.

lessons.title: Escapes in the runtime: runc CVE-2019-5736 and Leaky Vessels

blocks.md:
So far every escape was a setting someone chose. This lesson is about bugs in the code that builds the fences. **runc** is the low-level runtime underneath Docker, containerd, CRI-O and therefore most Kubernetes clusters: the program that actually creates namespaces, applies cgroups and starts the container's first process, following the OCI runtime specification. A bug in runc is a bug in every container's front door.

Both cases below share a pattern. For a brief moment while it sets up or enters a container, runc holds something that belongs to the host. If the container's code can reach that thing in that moment, the fence has a gap.

Where one shared kernel is too much trust (untrusted or multi-tenant code), clusters swap in a **sandboxed runtime**: gVisor, an application kernel written in Go that handles the container's system calls itself, or Kata Containers, which runs each pod in a lightweight virtual machine. Kubernetes selects one per pod with a RuntimeClass.

**Recall: runc CVE-2019-5736.** Disclosed on February 11, 2019 by Aleksa Sarai, a runc maintainer at SUSE, after researchers Adam Iwaniuk and Borys Popławski reported it. The [advisory](https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2019/02/11/2) says it "allows a malicious container to (with minimal user interaction) overwrite the host runc binary and thus gain root-level code execution on the host", when a root process in the container runs either from an attacker-controlled image or after an administrator does `docker exec` into a container the attacker could write to.

Mechanism, at concept level: while runc enters the container, the container can see the running runc process and, through `/proc`, a reference to runc's own executable, a host file. Writing through it replaces the host's runc, so the next use of runc runs attacker code as root on the host. Default AppArmor did not block it; user namespaces with host root unmapped did. The [fix](https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/commit/0a8e4117e7f715d5fbeef398405813ce8e88558b) ("clone /proc/self/exe to avoid exposing host binary to container") runs runc from a sealed in-memory copy (a `memfd`), leaving no host file to reach.

**Recall: Leaky Vessels, CVE-2024-21626, January 31, 2024.** The OS security course covered the bug; here is the fix and the disclosure in more depth. Rory McNamara of the security company Snyk found four container escape bugs that Snyk named "Leaky Vessels": this one in runc and three in BuildKit, Docker's image builder. The runc [advisory](https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/security/advisories/GHSA-xr7r-f8xq-vfvv) affects versions from 1.0.0-rc93 through 1.1.11; 1.1.12 fixes it.

The bug class is a **file descriptor leak** (CWE-403, "Exposure of File Descriptor to Unintended Control Sphere"). A file descriptor is a process's handle to an open file or directory. runc opened a handle to the host's `/sys/fs/cgroup` directory and failed to close it before starting the container's process. The container's working directory could be set to a path that resolves through that leftover handle, so the new process started with its current directory **in the host's filesystem**, outside the container's root. From there, relative paths walk the host.

blocks.title: Leaky Vessels at concept level: a leftover handle becomes a way out

scenes.caption: runc init is setting up the container. Earlier it opened a handle to the host's /sys/fs/cgroup for its own work.
It joins the container's namespaces and switches root to the container's filesystem. But the cgroup handle was never closed: it still points at a host directory.
The image (or an exec request) sets the working directory to a path that resolves through that open handle. chdir succeeds, and nothing checks where it landed.
The container's process starts with its current directory on the host. Relative paths from there reach the host filesystem: the fence was bypassed, not broken.

runc 1.1.12: verify the working directory is inside the container (getcwd fails with ENOENT if not), close all non-standard descriptors before exec, and mark descriptors close-on-exec. The path now ends at the container root.

blocks.title: The fix in runc 1.1.12, as a simplified model

scenes.caption: runc init has joined the container's namespaces and pivoted to the container's root. Before 1.1.12 a host directory handle was still open.
chdir to the configured working directory. If that path resolves through the leaked handle, this succeeds and lands on the host.
Fix 1: ask the kernel for the current directory. Linux returns ENOENT when it lies outside the process's root, so runc refuses to start the process.
Fix 2 (normal path): close or mark close-on-exec every descriptor above 2 before exec, so no host handle survives into the container even if a leak creeps back in.
Only now exec the container's program. It starts inside its root with only standard input, output and error open.
scenes.output: container process running, no host handles

blocks.md:
How bad was it, and who could trigger it? The advisory describes four attack variants. Some need a user to run a malicious image (or, with Docker, to build from a malicious Dockerfile or base image; Snyk's write-up centres on the WORKDIR instruction). Others work from inside an already running container when an administrator runs `runc exec` with a working directory. The highest score was CVSS 8.6. The advisory's own workarounds: only run trusted images, and only allow a working directory of `/`.

Disclosure was coordinated across the whole ecosystem. Snyk's [timeline](https://snyk.io/blog/leaky-vessels-docker-runc-container-breakout-vulnerabilities/) runs from discovery in the week of November 20, 2023 to a public release on January 31, 2024, when runc 1.1.12, containerd 1.6.28, Docker Engine 25.0.2 and 24.0.9, and cloud provider updates all shipped the same day. Snyk also released runtime and static detectors, and reported finding no evidence of exploitation in its checks.

blocks.title: Leaky Vessels coordinated disclosure (days after discovery week)

scenes.caption: Week of Nov 20, 2023: Rory McNamara finds the bugs and builds proofs of concept to confirm them.
Dec 11 (day 21): Snyk reports to Docker, which acknowledges the same day. Dec 12: Docker asks that the WORKDIR bug go to runc, since it lives there.
Jan 2 (day 43): CVE-2024-21626 is assigned. Jan 17 (day 58): runc notifies its security mailing list with patches and an embargo date.
Jan 31 (day 72): public disclosure. runc 1.1.12, containerd, Docker and cloud providers release on the same day, so defenders can patch before details spread.

blocks.md: Defender view. Prevent: patch runc, containerd and Docker on nodes and build machines; run only images from your signed pipeline; use user namespaces (`hostUsers: false`), which per the Kubernetes docs made several high and critical bugs unexploitable. Detect: Falco has a rule, off by default, for writes to /proc/self/exe (the CVE-2019-5736 pattern). Respond: a successful escape means the whole node is compromised.

Runtime escapes come from the runtime briefly holding host resources while entering a container. Patch the runtime everywhere, run only trusted images, and use user namespaces so that even a successful escape lands as an unprivileged user.

blocks.question: Which control blocked CVE-2019-5736 even on unpatched runc, according to the advisory?
options: User namespaces where the host's root is not mapped into the container
blocks.explain: The advisory says it is not blocked by the default AppArmor policy but is blocked by correct use of user namespaces: container root is then not host root, so it cannot write the host runc binary.

blocks.question: The runc 1.1.12 fix includes both a working-directory check and closing all non-standard descriptors before exec. Why both?
options: The descriptor close alone is too slow
Defence in depth: the cwd check blocks the working-directory attacks and closing descriptors blocks the program-path attacks, each even if a descriptor leaks
The check only works on Windows
One is for Docker, one for Kubernetes
blocks.explain: The advisory lists four fixes. Checking that the cwd is inside the container eliminates attacks 1 and 2 even if a descriptor leaks; closing internal descriptors right before execve eliminates attacks 3a and 3b, where a leaked handle is used in the program path. The other two close the specific leaks and mark descriptors close-on-exec against future leaks.

lessons.title: Runtime detection with Falco and the Kubernetes audit log

blocks.md:
Prevention fails eventually: a new runtime bug, a misconfigured namespace, a stolen token. **Detection** is how you find out in minutes instead of when the cloud bill arrives. In a cluster you need two views, because they see different things:

- The **Kubernetes audit log** (lesson 7) sees every request to the API server: who created a pod, who read Secrets, who added a ClusterRoleBinding, who ran `kubectl exec`.
- **Runtime detection** on each node sees what processes actually do: a shell spawned in a container, a file written to a sensitive path, an outbound connection to a mining pool. It sees activity that never touches the API server.

**Falco** is the common open source runtime detector. Its [docs](https://falco.org/docs/) describe it as "a cloud native security tool that provides runtime security across hosts, containers, Kubernetes, and cloud environments", originally created by Sysdig, a container security company, and now a graduated CNCF (Cloud Native Computing Foundation) project. It parses system calls from the kernel as they happen, adds container and Kubernetes context (image, pod, namespace), and evaluates them against **rules**.

A rule is a YAML object with at least `rule`, `desc`, `condition`, `output` and `priority`. The condition is a Boolean expression over event fields; the output is a message with `%field` placeholders. Falco's priority guidance: writing state is ERROR, unauthorized reads are WARNING, unexpected behaviour such as a shell in a container is NOTICE.

blocks.code:
# From the Falco docs: alert on each shell started in a container
- rule: shell_in_container
  desc: notice shell activity within a container
  condition: >
    (evt.type in (execve, execveat)) and
    container.id != host and
    (proc.name = bash or
     proc.name = ksh)
  output: >
    shell in a container |
    user=%user.name container_id=%container.id container_name=%container.name
    shell=%proc.name parent=%proc.pname cmdline=%proc.cmdline
  priority: WARNING

# A custom rule for the Hildegard hiding trick (lesson 13)
- rule: Write to ld.so.preload in container
  desc: A container process opened /etc/ld.so.preload for writing, a library injection technique used to hide processes
  condition: >
    evt.type in (open, openat, openat2) and evt.is_open_write = true and
    container.id != host and fd.name = /etc/ld.so.preload
  output: >
    ld.so.preload written in container |
    user=%user.name image=%container.image.repository ns=%k8s.ns.name
    pod=%k8s.pod.name cmdline=%proc.cmdline
  priority: ERROR
blocks.caption: The first rule is the Falco documentation's example (it uses WARNING, although the guidance would rate a shell NOTICE). The second uses only fields from Falco's supported-fields reference; it is ERROR because it writes state.

blocks.md:
Falco ships a default rule set; names worth knowing from its [default rules list](https://falco.org/docs/reference/rules/default-rules/) include "Terminal shell in container", "Drop and execute new binary in container" (a program that was not in the image's layers is executed: a read-only root filesystem makes this rarer and its alerts louder), "Contact K8S API Server From Container", "Contact cloud metadata service from container", "Launch Privileged Container", and several crypto-miner rules. Some are disabled by default or carry sandbox or incubating maturity tags, so read the tags before relying on one.

Why kernel-level matters: Hildegard hid its miner with LD_PRELOAD so that `ps` and `top` inside the container did not list it. A system call sensor on the node does not ask the container's userspace what is running; it sees the `execve` and the network connection directly.

blocks.title: One intrusion, three sensors: what each one sees

scenes.caption: Minute 0: the attacker uses an anonymous kubelet to exec into a container (the Hildegard pattern). Times are illustrative.
Falco on the node sees a shell spawned in the container right away. The API audit log sees nothing: the request went straight to the kubelet, never through the API server.
Minutes 2 to 6: tools are downloaded and run, and ld.so.preload is written to hide them. Falco flags a new binary not in the image and the preload write.
Minutes 6 to 14: scanning for more kubelets. Network flow logs show one pod opening connections to port 10250 across the node range.

Minute 14 on: miners run and connect to a pool. Falco's miner rules and egress logs fire. Had the attacker used a stolen token through the API server instead, the audit log would be the sensor that saw it.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages:
  - "RequestReceived"
rules:
  # Secrets and ConfigMaps: who touched them, never their values
  - level: Metadata
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]
  # RBAC changes: record the full object, they are rare and critical
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
    - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
      resources: ["clusterrolebindings", "rolebindings", "clusterroles", "roles"]
  # Pod creation and exec, with the request body (privileged? hostPath?)
  - level: Request
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["pods", "pods/exec"]
  # Everything else: metadata only
  - level: Metadata
blocks.caption: Built from the structure of the documentation's example policy. Pass it with --audit-policy-file and a log or webhook backend, and ship the events off the control plane.

blocks.md: Audit-log signals worth an alert, each tied to an earlier lesson: a new ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin (lesson 8); `list` or `watch` on Secrets by a service account that never did it before (lessons 8, 12); pods created with privileged, hostPID, hostNetwork or hostPath (lesson 5); `pods/exec` into production; TokenRequest calls for service accounts by unusual users (lesson 9); requests from `system:anonymous` that succeed. And the blind spot: direct kubelet API calls and `nodes/proxy` bypass the audit log's view of pod exec, which is one more reason the node needs its own sensor.

Misconception: "we have audit logging, so we would see an attack". The audit log sees API requests. An attacker who never calls the API server (kubelet exec, a runtime escape, a miner in an existing pod) leaves no audit events. Pair it with node-level runtime detection and network flow logs.
Use both views: the audit log for who changed what through the API, and a syscall-level sensor such as Falco for what processes actually do. Each covers the other's blind spot.

blocks.question: Inside a compromised container, `ps aux` shows nothing unusual, yet the node's CPU is high. Falco reports a known miner process in that pod. Which explanation fits best?
options: The attacker hid the process from userspace tools inside the container (for example with an LD_PRELOAD library), but the kernel-level sensor still sees the exec
The audit log hid the process
The miner runs on a different node
Falco is wrong because ps is authoritative
blocks.explain: Userspace inside a compromised container can lie. Hildegard filtered /proc reads through ld.so.preload. A sensor reading system calls from the kernel does not depend on the container's userspace.

blocks.question: Which event would appear in the Kubernetes audit log but not necessarily in Falco?
options: A shell spawned in a container through an anonymous kubelet
A service account listing all Secrets through the API server
A miner connecting to a pool
blocks.explain: Listing Secrets is an API request, recorded by the audit log, and produces no unusual process activity on a node for a syscall sensor to see. The others happen on nodes, outside the API server.

lessons.title: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise

blocks.md:
Each case in this course was stopped, or would have been, by a specific control. Lining them up shows why defence in depth works: every attack needed several things to go wrong, and each control removes one of them.

The Kubernetes project keeps a [security checklist](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/security-checklist/); it says checklists "are not sufficient for attaining a good security posture on their own", but they are a good first pass. The CIS (Center for Internet Security) Kubernetes Benchmark is a longer, scored list, and kube-bench, an open source tool from Aqua Security, checks a cluster against it. Grouped by this course's lessons:

1. **Images and build**: minimal or distroless bases, multi-stage builds, scanning in CI and while running, secret mounts instead of build args, no `ADD` from URLs without `--checksum`, a non-root `USER`.
2. **Supply chain**: pin images by digest, sign in CI, verify signatures at admission, protect the CI system as production.
3. **Pod settings**: Restricted Pod Security everywhere for apps; no privileged, hostPath, host namespaces or runtime sockets; seccomp RuntimeDefault, drop ALL, read-only root, no privilege escalation, user namespaces where supported.

4. **API access**: RBAC least privilege with namespaced Roles, no wildcards, no `system:masters` after bootstrap, periodic `can-i --list` reviews, automount off by default.
5. **Network**: default deny both ways in every namespace; API server, kubelet, etcd and dashboards off the internet; pods blocked from the cloud metadata address.
6. **Secrets and cloud**: encryption at rest with KMS, tight RBAC on Secrets, external stores for high-value credentials, workload identity instead of static keys.
7. **Nodes and runtime**: kubelet anonymous auth off with Webhook authorization; runc and containerd patched.
8. **Detection**: audit logging on and shipped off-cluster; Falco or similar on every node; egress and billing anomaly alerts.

blocks.title: Each real case and the control that breaks its chain

scenes.caption: Five cases from this course on the left, controls on the right. Each case needed a gap; each control closes one.
Tesla 2018: an unauthenticated console plus AWS keys in a pod. Authentication on management UIs breaks step one; workload identity removes the static keys it found.
Hildegard 2021: anonymous kubelets, then lateral scanning. Kubelet authentication stops entry; network policy stops the fan-out to other nodes' kubelets from pods.

IngressNightmare 2025: an unauthenticated admission webhook reachable from any pod. Patching fixed the bug, and since ingress-nginx was retired in 2026 the lasting fix is migrating; network policy limiting the webhook to the API server removes the reach.
runc 2019 and Leaky Vessels 2024: runtime bugs. Patching closes them; trusted, signed images from your own build remove the malicious-image route.
Codecov 2021: a key in an intermediate image layer. Build hygiene (secret mounts, multi-stage, layer secret scanning) stops the key from shipping at all.

blocks.code:
# A quick self-review of one cluster (read-only commands)
kubectl get ns --show-labels | grep pod-security          # which namespaces enforce what?
kubectl get networkpolicy -A                               # any namespace with none is default-allow
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide | grep cluster-admin
kubectl auth can-i --list --as system:serviceaccount:shop:default -n shop
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[?(@.spec.hostNetwork==true)]}{.metadata.namespace}/{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}'
blocks.caption: Each line checks one row of the map. The last prints every pod using the node's network namespace. Run these only against clusters you own or are authorised to assess.

blocks.md: Legal line: everything in this course is for clusters you own or have written permission to test. Scanning the internet for open kubelets or Docker APIs, or using one you find, is unauthorised access under laws such as the US CFAA and the UK Computer Misuse Act, whatever the intent.

**Where to practise legally.**

- [Kubernetes Goat](https://github.com/madhuakula/kubernetes-goat): an intentionally vulnerable cluster you run locally, by Madhu Akula, with scenarios including secrets hidden in image layers, container escape to the host, RBAC misconfiguration, namespace bypass and analysing a crypto miner container.
- [OWASP WrongSecrets](https://github.com/OWASP/wrongsecrets): an OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) game of real-life examples of how not to store secrets, with challenges across source code, Docker containers, Kubernetes and cloud deployments.
- [Kubernetes security tutorials](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/security/): official walk-throughs for Pod Security Standards at cluster and namespace level, seccomp and AppArmor, on a local cluster.
- Your own cluster: create one with kind or minikube, apply the hardened pod spec, the default-deny policies and a Restricted namespace label from this course, then try to break your own rules and read what the audit log and Falco record.

No single control holds. Minimal signed images, Restricted pods, least-privilege RBAC, default-deny networks, encrypted and narrowly readable Secrets, authenticated node APIs, patched runtimes, and two kinds of detection: each covers what the others miss.

blocks.question: A team can do one thing this week on a cluster with no network policies, Baseline pod security, and ingress-nginx admission webhooks. Which change shrinks the most attack paths from a single compromised pod?
options: Default-deny network policies with explicit allows, including restricting the webhook to the API server
blocks.explain: Under default allow, any pod can reach every service, admin webhook and node port. Default deny turns one foothold into a contained one and directly blocks the IngressNightmare path. Distroless helps too, but only for the images you rebuild.

blocks.question: Which pair of controls together would have prevented both the Tesla and the Hildegard initial access?
options: Requiring authentication on every management interface (consoles, kubelets) and keeping them off the internet
blocks.explain: Both started from a management interface that accepted unauthenticated requests from the internet. Authentication plus network exposure control closes that door; the other controls matter later in the chain.
